title: Git diff and stash
idea: `git diff` shows what changed between two of Git's three areas. `git stash` shelves uncommitted changes so you can switch tasks with a clean tree.

analogy.text: Your desk is the working tree, the outbox is staging, the filing cabinet is the last commit.
analogy.breaks: Staging copies a file; the desk copy stays where it is.

points: Changes move through three areas: working tree, staging area, last commit.
Plain `git diff` compares the working tree with the staging area.
`git diff --staged` compares the staging area with the last commit.
`git stash` shelves changes to tracked files, staged or not, and cleans the tree.

steps.caption: app.txt is committed with price 10. All three areas hold the same file.
You edit the file. Only the working tree changes.
`git diff` compares the working tree with the staging area.
`git add` copies the change into the staging area. Now plain `git diff` would print nothing.
`git diff --staged` compares the staging area with the last commit.
`git stash` moves the change to the stash. Working tree and staging area match the last commit again.
`git stash pop` returns the change to the working tree and drops the entry. It comes back unstaged.

code.title: Diff, then stash
code.caption: Press Run. Compare the two diffs, then the status lines before and after the stash.

walk.text: Create a repository with one commit, then edit the file to price 12.
`git diff` prints the edit: working tree against staging area.
After `git add`, the same edit shows under `--staged`: staging area against last commit.
`git stash` leaves a clean tree, so `git status --short` prints nothing.
The stash holds one entry, labelled with the commit it was made on.
`git stash pop` restores the edit. Status shows it unstaged: a space, then `M`.

pitfalls: A bare `git diff` prints nothing after `git add`; use `git diff --staged` instead.
`git stash` skips files Git has never tracked; add `-u` to include them.
`git stash pop` restores changes unstaged; add `--index` to keep them staged.

quiz.q: What does the last command print?
quiz.code:
# app.txt is committed with the text v1
echo "v2" > app.txt
git add app.txt
echo "v3" > app.txt
git diff
quiz.why: Plain `git diff` compares the working tree (v3) with the staging area (v2). The committed v1 is not involved.

takeaway: Diff before you commit; stash when you must switch with unfinished work.
